sights.name: Bratska Mogila (Brotherly Mound)
sights.blurb: At the western end of Boulevard 6 Septemvri a low, wide ring of stacked concrete slabs rises out of a lawn, echoing the Thracian burial mounds that dot the plain around Plovdiv.
sights.when: Exterior free and always open, with graffiti. The hall inside has been locked since about 1990; visitors report a caretaker with keys who is sometimes nearby. A restoration design has been tendered, but there was no money for works as of about 2025.

sights.name: Trakiya estate (252 blocks)
sights.blurb: Trakiya is the whole socialist city in one place: 252 blocks on the south-east edge of Plovdiv, begun in 1973 by a team under the architect Ivan Popov, and once home to about 62,000 people.
sights.when: Lived-in. The pin is the centre of the estate, not a single building.

sights.name: Trakiya, block 15 mosaics
sights.blurb: Two façade mosaics on block 15, signed “AK” for Anastasia Kmetova, made in 1973 and restored since.
sights.when: Restored. On the façade of a block by the old district hall.

sights.name: Mosaic fountain, Trakiya polyclinic
sights.blurb: A three-dimensional mosaic water feature in front of the Trakiya polyclinic (Saedinenie 42), made in the 1980s by Nedelchev and Tomova. It is in sound condition, mossy in places, and was cleaned in 2023.
sights.when: Sound but mossy; cleaned in 2023.

sights.name: Tobacco Town warehouses
sights.blurb: A district of brick warehouses and former tobacco-processing houses around Odrin Street, Hristo Botev Boulevard and Ivan Vazov Street, built between 1912 and 1932 by the architect Kamen Petkov.
sights.when: Street view only; do not go in. A private theatre is reported to be opening in the area (October 2026).

sights.name: Youth Hill (Dzhendem Tepe)
sights.blurb: The hill at the west end of the city centre, with a road made of concrete cubes laid by volunteer brigades from 1948, a decrepit hilltop pool, and a crown of antennas.
sights.when: Free and open.

sights.name: Disused railway strip
sights.blurb: A diagonal pedestrian corridor where railway tracks were taken up, a small cousin of Paris's Petite Ceinture.
sights.when: Location precision unverified; the pin is approximate.

sights.name: Kino Kosmos
sights.blurb: A 1960s modernist cinema on Gladstone Street, designed by Lyuben Bonev and Lubomir Shinkov and built in 1960–64, with a roof that was meant to retract and never did.
sights.when: Under reconstruction since June 2026; opening expected in summer 2027. Look at it from the street.

sights.name: House of Science and Technology
sights.blurb: A late-brutalist building by the Tsar Simeon Garden, by the architect M. Sapundzhiev, finished in 1985: an exposed concrete frame with terraces stepping toward the park.
sights.when: Open, with a café-bar and cinema inside (hours unverified).
sights.q: Dom na nauka i tehnika, ul. Gladstone 1, Plovdiv

sights.name: Youth House (now Council Hall)
sights.blurb: A huge cantilevered concrete volume over the entrance, built in the 1970s to a design by V. Rakshiev as the Dom na mladezhta, the House of Youth.
sights.when: In use. A 2025–26 proposal to cover its concrete wall with a mosaic has not been approved.

sights.name: Central Square: Party House, Trimontium, Post Office
sights.blurb: Three different decades of the regime's taste around one square.
sights.when: All in use; the Post Office hall is open to walk through during working hours.

sights.name: Ivan Vazov National Library
sights.blurb: The national library of Plovdiv, built in 1974, in stone cladding with bas-reliefs, stained glass and a mural. It sits at Avksentiy Veleshki 17 and is on the shortlist of the New Architectural Heritage project.
sights.when: Open on weekdays (winter reading rooms 08:00–17:45); entry to the reading rooms by reader card, so ask at the desk.

sights.name: Alyosha, Bunardzhik
sights.blurb: An 11-metre statue of a Soviet soldier on top of Bunardzhik Hill, put up in 1954–57 to honour the Red Army and nicknamed Alyosha. It has been the object of removal attempts in 1989 and 1996, and it is still there.
sights.when: Free and open.

sights.name: International Fair: pavilions and the Mercury mosaic
sights.blurb: The fair grounds on the river side of town, with pavilions from the era of the Plovdiv fairs, the Eastern Bloc's trade showcase.
sights.when: Fair grounds; open during events, otherwise the perimeter.

sights.name: Yuri Gagarin mosaic wall
sights.blurb: A mosaic wall at the roundabout by the fair, with a flying figure, three dates and a hole through the middle of the wall.
sights.when: Stable, with graffiti and lost tesserae. The pin is from the address; the register's own coordinates contradict it, so check the spot on Street View.

sights.name: Rowing canal and Stadion Plovdiv
sights.blurb: A 2.2-km rowing canal with a grandstand for about 800 spectators, in a park west of the city, and next to it the Stadion Plovdiv, opened in 1950 (the architect was Vladimir Rangelov, and it was first called the “9 September” stadium).
sights.when: Open.

sights.name: Monument to the Unification (1985)
sights.blurb: A concrete monument by Minekov and Lozanov from 1985 for the Unification of Bulgaria (1885, when the principality and Eastern Rumelia joined). The Regional History Museum, the 1885 Assembly building, is a short walk away.
sights.when: Free.

sights.name: Lotus Hall (House of the Newborn)
sights.blurb: A round oval hall of marble and glass in the Dondukov garden, built in 1973 as the “House of the Newborn”, a state ceremony hall for naming babies, designed by Dimka Taneva and Maria Sapundzhieva.
sights.when: Open as a natural-history museum with a dinosaur “cave” inside.
sights.q: Zala Lotos, Hristo G. Danov 34, Plovdiv

sights.name: House of the Newlyweds
sights.blurb: A glass-walled building from 1962 in the Dondukov garden, designed by an architect named Mihova, where civil wedding ceremonies were held.
sights.when: In use; an “Africa” exhibit downstairs.

sights.name: Mother and Child House
sights.blurb: The fourth of the regime's ritual buildings, opposite the Church of Sveta Petka. The research gives no present use, and the pin is approximate.
sights.when: Present use unknown; the pin is approximate.

sights.name: Design Organisation building (Prosecutor’s Office)
sights.blurb: A modernist building of the 1970s on Saedinenie Square where the city's architects worked, now the Prosecutor's Office. It is in use and on the edge of the centre. Pair it with the Regional History Museum opposite.
sights.when: In use; the pin is approximate.

sights.name: The “Big Giant” megablock, Karshiyaka
sights.blurb: The largest residential block in Plovdiv, about 2,000 residents, in the district of Karshiyaka across the river. The district mayor has called it the largest in the city. A passage is cut under the building where a flat should be.
sights.when: Lived-in. The pin is approximate: it is opposite the bus stop at Vasil Levski 96, next to Zala Stroitel.

sights.name: Novotel / Grand Hotel Plovdiv (ex-Hotel Maritsa)
sights.blurb: A big socialist-era river hotel by the fair, once the Hotel Maritsa, then a Novotel and now the Grand Hotel Plovdiv. It was built to put up foreign visitors to the fair.
sights.when: Operating.

sights.name: Hotel Sankt Peterburg (ex-Leningrad)
sights.blurb: A socialist-era hotel in Karshiyaka, formerly the Hotel Leningrad, named for Plovdiv's twin city. It is operating.
sights.when: Operating.

sights.name: University of Food Technologies
sights.blurb: The rectorate building of the university has a large sgraffito (scratched plaster) decoration of the 1970s–80s. It is in use.
sights.when: In use.

sights.name: Zala Stroitel (steel sports hall)
sights.blurb: A steel-framed sports hall (about 2,200 tonnes of steel) on Karlovsko shose, beside Ribnitsa park. Early reports called it a possible ruin; it is not, and national volleyball finals were held there in April 2026.
sights.when: An active sports hall (national volleyball finals in April 2026), not a ruin.

sights.name: Dumped socialist statues, Sheker mahala
sights.blurb: Behind a wire fence in the yard of the former Metalni Konstruktsii company, on Vasil Levski Street in Sheker mahala, lie the statues that Plovdiv removed from its streets in 1991–96.
sights.when: Fenced; you can only look through the wire. The exact gate has not been found, so the pin is approximate.

sights.name: Avtogara Sever (North Bus Station)
sights.blurb: A 1970 bus station by the Filipovo railway station that looks closed and is not quite: a visitor in July 2026 reported that the building seems shut but buses still run, with tickets sold by drivers.
sights.when: Half-closed, but buses still run (tickets from the drivers, July 2026). The city council discussed the station in May 2026; the building is at risk.

sights.name: Filipovo station and old industrial zone
sights.blurb: Half-collapsed buildings around the 1915 Filipovo station, which is itself ordinary. The old industrial zone behind the bus station is the nearest thing in the city to a ruin you can see from the street.
sights.when: Ruins partly collapsed; keep to the street.

sights.name: Spartak stadium (Todor Diev)
sights.blurb: A football ground in Kyuchuk Parizh, built in 1925–26 and rebuilt in 1984–86, reported in recent reviews as neglected and falling apart, awaiting renovation. Earlier sources conflict between decay and construction.
sights.when: Decaying; waiting for renovation.

sights.name: September Uprising memorial and mosaic
sights.blurb: A memorial complex for the September 1923 uprising, on Peshtersko shose 149 in the Smirnenski district, with a mosaic by Georgi Boyadzhiev and the architect Antoaneta Topalova from about 1983.
sights.when: Unmaintained, with graffiti, moss and flaking tesserae.

sights.name: Plovdiv–Leningrad mosaic
sights.blurb: A natural-stone mosaic from the 1980s on Knyaz Aleksandar I Street, number 44, given to Plovdiv by artists from its twin city of Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). It is stable but partly hidden by shop awnings, so look up.
sights.when: Stable, but partly hidden by shop awnings.

sights.name: Bunardzhika bomb shelter
sights.blurb: A Cold War tunnel at the south foot of Bunardzhik Hill, one of two shelters in Plovdiv kept in order. It was reopened in 2026 as a venue for an exhibition on “Lost Spaces” and a public talk on 12 September 2026.
sights.when: Open only for events (an exhibition and a talk in September 2026). The entrance is at the south foot of the hill; the exact door is not published, so the pin is approximate.

sights.name: Sahat Tepe shelters
sights.blurb: Three shelters in the hill under the clock tower. The civil-defence education centre behind Radio Plovdiv is open only during the annual civil-defence competition. The shelter next door is a working restaurant.
sights.when: Closed. The civil-defence centre opens only for the annual competition; the shelter next door is a restaurant; “Skalata” is abandoned. The pin is approximate.

sights.name: Peshterata cave shelter
sights.blurb: A rock-face shelter by the Monday market (Ponedelnik pazar) at the foot of Dzhambaz Tepe, once a cave restaurant. It is closed and locked. A second shelter, “Nonstop”, by the cathedral in the Old Town, is also locked.
sights.when: Closed and locked. The pin is approximate.

sights.name: Central Cemetery
sights.blurb: A large cemetery east of the centre, with different communities side by side: Orthodox, Armenian, Catholic, Jewish and Muslim, plus war graves.
sights.when: Open daily, about 07:00–21:00.

sights.name: Old Town tunnel portal reliefs
sights.blurb: Stone reliefs at both ends of the road tunnel below the Old Town. At the south entrance a large relief of Hebros and Thrace, from a project by Anastasia Kmetova.
sights.when: Partly overgrown. The pin is the south portal, from a bus stop; the north portal is near 42.1505, 24.7498.

sights.name: Saborna sgraffiti
sights.blurb: A set of sgraffiti (scratched-plaster murals) on Saborna Street and nearby, including the Zahari Zograf and Orpheus panels (early 1970s, Dimitar Kirov, called Di Kiro), a Thracian rider over the Encho Pironkov house, and a 10 by 13 metre wall by Georgi Bozhilov (1968) next to the Church of the Assumption.
sights.when: Visible from the street; pin approximate.

sights.name: Underpass mosaics at Banya Starinna
sights.blurb: Mosaics by Yoan Leviev (1969) in the underpass at Tsar Boris III Obedinitel 54, beside the Chifte Hamam. They were restored in 2020 and have had paint and dirt on them since.
sights.when: Restored in 2020; paint and dirt since.

sights.name: Gerdzhika bridge
sights.blurb: A bridge of five 30-metre concrete arches, built in 1930–31 by Kamen Velkov and paid for by donations after the Chirpan earthquake. A twin was built alongside in 2008 with a one-metre gap between them.
sights.when: In use.

sights.name: Burago’s ford memorial
sights.blurb: A concrete pyramid and a stone “Thracian plain” pavement about 9 km west of the city on the Pazardzhik road, built in 1970 to mark where Captain Burago’s cavalry is said to have crossed the Maritsa in January 1878.
sights.when: Renewed in 2009. About 9 km west.

sights.name: Markovo Tepe (the quarried hill)
sights.blurb: A shopping mall stands where Plovdiv's “seventh hill” used to be. Markovo Tepe was quarried away for syenite paving stones, and you have walked on it if you have walked on the city's cobbles.
sights.when: A shopping mall stands on it.

sights.name: Roman stadium in a shop basement
sights.blurb: A section of the Roman stadium of Philippopolis, the long racetrack under the main street, is said to be visible inside a shop near Dzhumaya Square. Verify on the spot; the research flagged this as unconfirmed.
sights.when: A section is said to be visible inside a shop; verify on the spot.

sights.name: Youth Hill children’s railway
sights.blurb: A communist-era children's railway with four wagons on Youth Hill, seasonal and with unverified running days. The Pioneer railways were a standard piece of the regime's youth programme.
sights.when: Seasonal; running days unverified.

sights.name: Pop Nikola Belchov plaque
sights.blurb: An open-book relief by the sculptor Viktor Todorov on the colonnade of Knyaz Aleksandar I Street, near the spot where the priest Nikola Belchov was hanged in July 1876 after the April Uprising was crushed.
sights.when: The bronze head was stolen and later returned.

sights.name: Former Jewish school and Monument of Gratitude
sights.blurb: On 10 March 1943 the Bulgarian authorities began rounding up Plovdiv's Jews for deportation, and held them in the yard of this school.
sights.when: A plaque and a 1998 monument; pin approximate.

sights.name: Zion synagogue
sights.blurb: A synagogue built in 1886–87 and used as a warehouse under communism. Plaques honour Metropolitan Kiril and Dimitar Peshev, the deputy speaker of parliament who intervened to stop the deportations.
sights.when: Reached through a courtyard; Google lists Monday–Friday 10:00–13:00, and one visitor reported no free passage. Ask first.

sights.name: Chifte Hamam (Banya Starinna)
sights.blurb: A twin-domed Ottoman bathhouse of 1582, with reused Roman stones in its walls and incised builders' drawings, on Boulevard 6 Septemvri. It is one of the best Ottoman buildings in Plovdiv and for a long time worked as a gallery.
sights.when: Closed since 2023 for structural risk, damp and falling plaster; exterior only.

sights.name: Orta Mezar (Eni Hamam) ruin
sights.blurb: A fire-gutted shell of a 15th–16th-century Ottoman bath at the corner of Ruski and 6 Septemvri, west of the Dondukov garden. A demolition order of 1929 was never carried out.
sights.when: A burnt shell; view from the street. The pin is approximate.

sights.name: Political prisoners’ memorial (gallows site)
sights.blurb: On Boulevard Bulgaria, to the right of the Hotel Sankt Peterburg, stood a raw-concrete labyrinth by Viktor Todorov from the 1980s on the site of the old gallows, for the political prisoners killed there.
sights.when: A remnant, and it may be gone: the sculptor’s site says the bronze figure is lost and most walls were demolished. The pin is approximate.
sights.q: bul. Bulgaria, next to Hotel Sankt Peterburg, Plovdiv

sights.name: Sasho Sladura statue
sights.blurb: A statue of the jazz violinist Sasho Sladura by the Music Academy and the Ancient Theatre. He was a dissident musician who died in the Lovech labour camp in 1961. You can sit on his knee, and people do.
sights.when: Free; you can sit on his knee.

sights.name: Clock tower, Sahat Tepe
sights.blurb: A wooden clock tower on this spot by 1611, rebuilt in stone in 1809–12, with a Viennese clock from 1883.
sights.when: Open about 08:00–18:00.

sights.name: Hippocrates pharmacy museum
sights.blurb: The only pharmacy museum in Bulgaria, opened in 1981 at Saborna 16, in an Old Town house. Sources give its opening date as 1872 or 1882. Open Tuesday–Sunday.
sights.when: Open Tuesday–Sunday.

sights.name: Roman aqueduct, Komatevsko shose
sights.blurb: A stretch of Roman aqueduct in the middle of the Komatevsko shose road. Height and date are disputed between sources (up to about 14 metres per one source, 6–8 per another; 5th–6th century against 2nd–3rd).
sights.when: Free, in the middle of the road.

sights.name: Eastern Gate and Hadzhi Hasan mahala
sights.blurb: The Eastern Gate of the Roman and later city wall at Aleksandar Malinov Square, with the 15th-century Hadzhi Hasan mahala (neighbourhood) next to it, still with horse carts.
sights.when: Free; open about 07:00–18:30.

sights.name: Late-antique building “Irini”
sights.blurb: A late-antique building with mosaics shown in place inside a road underpass at Tsar Boris III Obedinitel 89. It is open daily 09:00–18:00 and costs about €2–3.50.
sights.when: Open daily 09:00–18:00; about €2–3.50.

sights.name: Thrakart Roman mosaics
sights.blurb: Roman mosaics behind glass walls in the Tsar Boris III underpass, in the Thrakart (Tracart) cultural centre, which belongs to Georges Trak, the sculptor who collected the dumped statues. You can see them from the underpass.
sights.when: Seen through glass from the underpass; pin approximate.

sights.name: The “Heap of our discontent”
sights.blurb: A pile of stones in the Dondukov garden, put there in 1997 as a protest by an artist or group against the state of the garden. It is on the Hristo G. Danov Street side.
sights.when: Probably still there, but expected to be removed when the garden is renovated (not started by April 2026).
sights.q: Dondukov garden, Hristo G. Danov side, Plovdiv

sights.name: Captain Burago bust
sights.blurb: A bust in the Dondukov garden by Viktor Todorov (1969) of Captain Burago, the Russian cavalry officer credited with freeing Plovdiv in January 1878. Free; a minor stop.
sights.when: Free.

sights.name: Kamen Vichev statue
sights.blurb: A statue by Danko Dankov (2000) of Kamen Vichev, a Catholic priest shot in 1952, in the garden opposite Sveta Petka on Boulevard Maria Luiza. It may be unlabelled. Plaques have been reported but not confirmed.
sights.when: May be unlabelled; the pin is approximate.

sights.name: Raycho Nikolov plaque, Dzhumaya
sights.blurb: A 2005 plaque at the Dzhumaya mosque for Captain Raycho Nikolov, the only victim of the 1885 Unification; his grave is in plot 50A of the Central Cemetery. A minor stop.
sights.when: Free; pin approximate.

sights.name: 1885 Assembly building (Regional History Museum)
sights.blurb: The building of the Regional History Museum at Saedinenie Square was built as the assembly hall of Eastern Rumelia by Montani, but the assembly never used it.
sights.when: Open Monday–Saturday.

sights.name: Cosmonaut pines, Bunardzhik
sights.blurb: A row of pines on Bunardzhik said to have been planted in the 1960s by cosmonauts including Gagarin and Tereshkova. The research calls it probable, not confirmed. Pair it with Alyosha.
sights.when: Probably still growing; pin approximate.

sights.name: “House with the Tower”
sights.blurb: The former Second Police Station, built in 1904 and a police station from 1938, at Lady Strangford and Antim I streets. Now flats, decaying.
sights.when: Flats, decaying; pin approximate.

sights.name: Site of the Adzhemsko coffeehouse
sights.blurb: The place where a Persian (Adzhemsko) coffeehouse once stood, off Rayko Daskalov and Bogoridi streets. Nothing remains; it is the spot only, and a quick stop on the way.
sights.when: The spot only; pin approximate.

sights.name: Rock Bar Download (ex-Kafene Kristal)
sights.blurb: The Grand Café Kristal was the socialist-era writers' haunt of Plovdiv, a place for Gencho Stoev, Konstantin Pavlov and the actors of the Drama Theatre. It is described in a memoir, Georgi Raychevski's Grandkafe Kristal (1998).
sights.when: Open, but leaves this address on 31 December 2026; the building is for sale.
sights.q: Rock Bar Download, Lady Strangford 5, Plovdiv

sights.name: Kafene Starinnoto (Slaveykov’s café)
sights.blurb: A café on Vazrazhdane Square from the 1880s where the poet Petko Rachev Slaveykov drank his morning coffee; the original hearth survives. It closed in March 2026 for restoration, with no reopening date.
sights.when: Closed for restoration since March 2026, with no reopening date; pin approximate.

sights.name: Vazov’s gazebo, Lichev house
sights.blurb: A gazebo of 1913 where the writer Ivan Vazov spent his last birthday in 1920, in the yard of the Lichev house on Veliko Tarnovo Street. It is a private yard and access is unverified.
sights.when: A private yard; access unverified, pin approximate.

sights.name: Alafrangite restaurant
sights.blurb: An 18th-century house with painted alafranga niches, a restaurant that was a bohemian haunt in the 1960s, at K. Nektariev 17. The first research pass wrongly listed it as gone; it is open.
sights.when: Open.

sights.name: Zlatna Krusha (now a Thai kitchen)
sights.blurb: Built in 1929 by the architect Boyan Chinkov at Otets Paisiy 28, this was a haunt of bohemians and the intelligentsia. It is open today as a Thai kitchen.
sights.when: Open, as a Thai kitchen.

sights.name: Site of the First Shumen Beerhouse (now Unico)
sights.blurb: The First Shumen Beerhouse opened in 1913 at Otets Paisiy and General Gurko streets, and the intelligentsia met here after theatre premieres. It is now the restaurant Unico.
sights.when: Now the Unico restaurant.

sights.name: Tsanko Lavrenov bench statue
sights.blurb: A bronze of the painter Tsanko Lavrenov on a bench at Saborna 41, holding a picture frame. Free; sit beside him.
sights.when: Free.

offmap.name: Buzludzha
offmap.blurb: The great saucer-shaped Communist Party hall on Buzludzha peak (1,441 m), built 1974–81 to a design by Georgi Stoilov and one of the most photographed ruins in the world.
offmap.when: Exterior free; interior sealed and guarded (asbestos, cameras). Getty-funded conservation under way. About 2 hours by bus via Kazanlak, then a taxi or car; private tours from about €270 per vehicle.

offmap.name: Three Generations monument, Perushtitsa
offmap.blurb: The best find of the manual pass: a 60-metre stone-and-brick complex on Vlasevitsa hill, 1976, by the Bratska Mogila team (Shinkov, Rangelov and the sculptor Dalchev), with stepped terraces and reliefs, a bell tower, a light well and a crypt with an empty sarcophagus.
offmap.when: Open 24/7 on the hill; the crypt is locked. About 20 km south-west, by road.

offmap.name: Aviation Museum, Krumovo
offmap.blurb: A branch of the National Military History Museum at the old airfield of Krumovo, with about 66 aircraft outdoors, radar, a 1912 Bozhinov plane and a capsule of cosmonaut Georgi Ivanov. Open Wednesday–Sunday 09:00–18:00.

offmap.name: Mondi Stamboliyski pulp mill
offmap.blurb: A state pulp combine founded in 1952, idle since a fire on 24 September 2024 and closed in 2025, sold to a Plovdiv firm. View it from the road.
offmap.when: Closed since 2025 after a 2024 fire; sold on. View from outside only.

offmap.name: Defenders of Stara Zagora (Samara Flag)
offmap.blurb: A 1977 concrete flag monolith on three pillars with giant figures and an ossuary, on a hill at Stara Zagora, about 100 km east. Free; hours unverified.

offmap.name: Apriltsi memorial, Panagyurishte
offmap.blurb: A 1976 hillside memorial complex above Panagyurishte for the April Uprising of 1876, with a giant figure called Borimechkata. Free; about 70 km north-west.

offmap.name: Dimitrovgrad
offmap.blurb: Bulgaria's first socialist town, begun in 1947, with a Stalinist centre, a town hall of 1967 and a museum of “socialist construction”. Hours of the museum are unverified. About 100 km east.
offmap.when: A working town; the museum of “socialist construction” has unverified hours.

p: At the western end of Boulevard 6 Septemvri a low, wide ring of stacked concrete slabs rises out of a lawn, echoing the Thracian burial mounds that dot the plain around Plovdiv. It is the city's best piece of socialist monumental architecture and the first stop on the map for anyone who came for concrete. The outside is free and always open; the inside is the part you cannot see.

It was built in 1971–74 by the architects Lubomir Shinkov and Vladimir Rangelov, with reliefs by the sculptor Lubomir Dalchev, and opened on 9 September 1974, the thirtieth anniversary of the 1944 coup that brought the communists to power (celebrated as the “Ninth of September”). Inside is a hall with Dalchev's reliefs and a wall of bronze urns holding the remains of 126 partisans. The idea was a modern mound for the new regime's dead: a pagan, pre-Christian form chosen to feel older than any church.

The hall has been locked since about 1990 and the monument is covered in graffiti. Visitors report a caretaker with keys who is sometimes nearby, so it is worth asking, but do not count on it. A restoration design has been tendered, but as of about 2025 there was no money for the works. The monument is on the shortlist of the New Architectural Heritage of Plovdiv project.
The same team built the Three Generations monument at Perushtitsa two years later; if this one moves you, that one is the day trip to make.
bratska-mogila.s: nan.bg (New Architectural Heritage of Plovdiv); Wikidata; nonument.org; visitor reviews; lostinplovdiv.com

p: Trakiya is the whole socialist city in one place: 252 blocks on the south-east edge of Plovdiv, begun in 1973 by a team under the architect Ivan Popov, and once home to about 62,000 people. The pin is the middle of the estate, not a building. Nothing here is a ruin; people live in it, which is the point.

Walk it as an urban landscape rather than a list of sights: long slab blocks, courtyards, the lines of bus stops, the small shops at the foot of the blocks. There is a time capsule meant to be opened in 2111, but nobody has confirmed where it was put. Between blocks 1 and 3 is Pool Trakiya, reactivated in 2016 by the Austrian architect Gabu Heindl; its present state is unverified, so check before you make a trip for it.

The estate is also an art gallery without walls: block 15 carries a restored pair of mosaics by Anastasia Kmetova, and the polyclinic has a three-dimensional mosaic fountain (see those two stops). Take a bus or taxi from the centre; the distances inside the estate are long.
trakiya-estate.s: Wikipedia; lostinplovdiv.com; gabuheindl.at; nan.bg. Pool state unverified. Map pin is the estate centre.

p: Two façade mosaics on block 15, signed “AK” for Anastasia Kmetova, made in 1973 and restored since. They are the best-kept example of the art the regime put on its housing estates: big, colourful, abstract-figurative panels meant to be seen from a passing bus.

A three-dimensional mosaic water feature in front of the Trakiya polyclinic (Saedinenie 42), made in the 1980s by Nedelchev and Tomova. It is in sound condition, mossy in places, and was cleaned in 2023. The kind of thing you would never find without a register; pair it with block 15.

A district of brick warehouses and former tobacco-processing houses around Odrin Street, Hristo Botev Boulevard and Ivan Vazov Street, built between 1912 and 1932 by the architect Kamen Petkov. For half a century Plovdiv was one of the world's tobacco-trading cities, and this is where the leaf was sorted and packed. Today it is a half-empty brick quarter: some buildings renovated (the SKLAD complex, a useful contrast), some burnt out, like the Orient Tabaco shell at Odrin 8.

It is also the site of the 1953 tobacco-workers' revolt, though there is no plaque and no marker. On 3–4 May 1953, a few weeks after Stalin's death, workers protested over pay and conditions; troops fired, and sources give three to nine dead. It is often called the first uprising in the Eastern Bloc after Stalin died, but the number of victims is disputed and the event is poorly documented. Look at the buildings with that in mind: the history is in the street, not on a wall.

The quarter has been hit by a partial demolition and fire in 2016 and the demolition of the Kudoglu warehouse in 2018. Do not go inside any of the empty buildings; walk the streets and look. A private theatre is reported to be opening here (podtepeto, 28 October 2026).
tobacco-town.s: nan.bg; lostinplovdiv.com; theanarchistlibrary.org (1953 revolt); podtepeto.com (Oct 2026). Death toll disputed. Map pin approximate.

p: The hill at the west end of the city centre, with a road made of concrete cubes laid by volunteer brigades from 1948, a decrepit hilltop pool, and a crown of antennas. It is free and open and gives a good view over the city and the plain. The brigade movement, in which young people built roads and railways for free as a political duty, is a whole chapter of Bulgarian socialism, and this road is a small, physical piece of it.

A diagonal pedestrian corridor where railway tracks were taken up, a small cousin of Paris's Petite Ceinture. The research gives only a rough location and flags it as unverified, so treat it as a lead rather than a destination: look it up on a map before heading out. Sources do not agree on its precise route.
rail-strip.s: Master research pass (location unverified). Map pin approximate.

p: A 1960s modernist cinema on Gladstone Street, designed by Lyuben Bonev and Lubomir Shinkov and built in 1960–64, with a roof that was meant to retract and never did. It is one of the best modernist buildings in the city, and it was saved from demolition in 2010.

Reconstruction began in June 2026, with the 599-seat hall due to open in summer 2027, so for now you can only see it from outside, behind the works. Earlier reports of a late-2026 opening are out of date. Before the works it stood deserted for years after an earlier renovation.
Look at the façade and the way the building sits in the street; it is a good example of the optimism of the early 1960s, before the heavier concrete of the Party House era.
kino-kosmos.s: lostinplovdiv.com (12 Jun 2026); plovdiv24.bg; nan.bg. Opening date has moved more than once.

p: A late-brutalist building by the Tsar Simeon Garden, by the architect M. Sapundzhiev, finished in 1985: an exposed concrete frame with terraces stepping toward the park. It is on the shortlist of the New Architectural Heritage of Plovdiv project and one of the few such buildings you can walk into, because it houses a café-bar and a cinema (hours unverified).
Look at how it handles the slope toward the garden, and note the date: in 1985 the regime had four more years to run, and the building is the last confident statement of its style in the city.
Next to it is the garden where, according to local lore, the entrance to the 1892 Plovdiv exhibition stood; the Demeter fountain is said to mark the place. There is no plaque.
house-science.s: nan.bg; lostinplovdiv.com. Garden/exhibition note unverified (no plaque).

p: A huge cantilevered concrete volume over the entrance, built in the 1970s to a design by V. Rakshiev as the Dom na mladezhta, the House of Youth. It is now the Council Hall and in use, and it is on the shortlist of the New Architectural Heritage project.

The big blank concrete wall is the point. In 2025–26 a proposal to cover it with a mosaic was put forward, but nothing has been approved, so for now it remains one of the bare, heavy surfaces that make Plovdiv's centre look like it does.
youth-house.s: nan.bg; lostinplovdiv.com; D1 research pass (2025–26 mosaic proposal)

central-square.t: Central Square: Party House, Trimontium, Post Office
p: Three different decades of the regime's taste around one square. The 12-storey Party House (designed in 1965–66 and opened in April 1969) is the old communist headquarters and was nicknamed the Mother Party House; urban legend gives the first secretary a suite on the ninth floor. The Hotel Trimontium (1956, now a Ramada) is Stalinist: heavy, symmetrical, decorated. The Central Post Office has 1970s interiors and mosaics, and you can walk in during working hours.

The square is where Plovdiv's regime history reads most clearly: classical pretension in 1956, modernism in 1969, and a post office that still works. The name Trimontium comes from the ancient name for the city, “three hills”.
Walk through the Post Office hall before leaving: of the three, it is the one still doing the job it was built for.
central-square.s: nan.bg; lostinplovdiv.com. Party House detail from manual pass (28–29 Oct 2026).

p: The national library of Plovdiv, built in 1974, in stone cladding with bas-reliefs, stained glass and a mural. It sits at Avksentiy Veleshki 17 and is on the shortlist of the New Architectural Heritage project.

The reading rooms are open on weekdays (winter hours 08:00–17:45) and entry is by reader card, so ask at the desk if you want to see inside; the staff may let you look. Unlike the concrete elsewhere on this map, this is a building with warmth in it, and it still does exactly what it was built for.
library.s: nan.bg; libplovdiv.com; lostinplovdiv.com. Hours may have changed.

p: An 11-metre statue of a Soviet soldier on top of Bunardzhik Hill, put up in 1954–57 to honour the Red Army and nicknamed Alyosha. It has been the object of removal attempts in 1989 and 1996, and it is still there. The hill is free to climb and has a view of the whole city.
It is a famous icon, but a plain one, which is why the map ranks it below the concrete: you go for the hill, the shelter at its foot, the pines and the view, not for the statue alone.

fair.t: International Fair: pavilions and the Mercury mosaic
p: The fair grounds on the river side of town, with pavilions from the era of the Plovdiv fairs, the Eastern Bloc's trade showcase. Plovdiv held EXPO 1991, one of the last expos of the Eastern Bloc, and some of the pavilions are from that time. Look for the Mercury mosaic on the grounds, with the Gagarin wall just outside (see next stop). The grounds are open during events, otherwise you see the perimeter.

A mosaic wall at the roundabout by the fair, with a flying figure, three dates and a hole through the middle of the wall. It is the work of the artist Yoan Leviev from 1971, and one of the most striking pieces of socialist space-age art in the city. It is stable, with graffiti and lost tesserae.

Gagarin was the regime's hero because the Soviet space programme was the proof that the system worked. Bunardzhik hill has a row of pines said to have been planted in the 1960s by cosmonauts, and the same optimism is in the wall: the human figure launching off into space, in colour.

The register has a mismatch: the address (Tsar Boris III Obedinitel 33–37, at the first Fair roundabout) is right, but the coordinates it gave are near the rowing canal. The pin here follows the address; check it on Street View.
gagarin-wall.s: novotonasledstvo.eu; lostinplovdiv.com. Pin follows the address; coordinates in sources disagree.

p: A 2.2-km rowing canal with a grandstand for about 800 spectators, in a park west of the city, and next to it the Stadion Plovdiv, opened in 1950 (the architect was Vladimir Rangelov, and it was first called the “9 September” stadium). It is a big flat piece of socialist sports infrastructure. Go for the canal on a walk; there is not much else to see.

A concrete monument by Minekov and Lozanov from 1985 for the Unification of Bulgaria (1885, when the principality and Eastern Rumelia joined). The Regional History Museum, the 1885 Assembly building, is a short walk away. A minor stop.

A round oval hall of marble and glass in the Dondukov garden, built in 1973 as the “House of the Newborn”, a state ceremony hall for naming babies, designed by Dimka Taneva and Maria Sapundzhieva. It is part of the regime's attempt to replace church rites with socialist ones. A near-copy stands in Chișinău, built in 1979.

The marble was stripped from 2018 and since 1 December 2021 the interior has been a Natural History Museum “cave” with animatronic dinosaurs. It is socialist ritual architecture turned into kitsch, which is exactly why it is on the map: the transformation is the story.

It forms a group with the House of the Newlyweds next door, the Mother and Child House, and the House of the Deceased at the Central Cemetery. Together they are the regime's four secular rites: birth, marriage, motherhood, death.
lotus-hall.s: lostinplovdiv.com; podtepeto.com (Zala Lotos); manual pass (ritual houses theme)

p: A glass-walled building from 1962 in the Dondukov garden, designed by an architect named Mihova, where civil wedding ceremonies were held. The lower floor has been turned into an “Africa” exhibit with plasterboard decoration, against the architects' protests. It is still in use.
It is the second of the regime's ritual houses; see Lotus Hall next door for the first. The Orthodox church had been the place for weddings; the state wanted its own.

The fourth of the regime's ritual buildings, opposite the Church of Sveta Petka. The research gives no present use, and the pin is approximate. It is on the map for completeness, as part of the ritual-houses group with Lotus Hall, the Newlyweds and the Central Cemetery.
mother-child.s: Manual pass (28 Oct 2026). Use and pin unverified.

p: A modernist building of the 1970s on Saedinenie Square where the city's architects worked, now the Prosecutor's Office. It is in use and on the edge of the centre. Pair it with the Regional History Museum opposite.
design-org.s: lostinplovdiv.com (5 emblematic socialist buildings). Pin approximate.

p: The largest residential block in Plovdiv, about 2,000 residents, in the district of Karshiyaka across the river. The district mayor has called it the largest in the city. A passage is cut under the building where a flat should be.

There is a smaller sibling, the “Little Giant”, nearby. This is how a lot of Bulgarians lived and still live, and the point of the stop is to see the scale and the way a whole village-sized community uses the building. Be a visitor, not a photographer of residents' windows.
It is close to Zala Stroitel and the monument dump, so it fits one walk in Karshiyaka.
big-giant.s: plovdiv24.bg; bnr.bg. Pin approximate (opposite the stop at Vasil Levski 96).

p: A big socialist-era river hotel by the fair, once the Hotel Maritsa, then a Novotel and now the Grand Hotel Plovdiv. It was built to put up foreign visitors to the fair. It is operating, so you can go in; for most visitors, it is a landmark on the way to the Gagarin wall.

A socialist-era hotel in Karshiyaka, formerly the Hotel Leningrad, named for Plovdiv's twin city. It is operating. It is also the landmark for the political prisoners' memorial, which is just to its right, and it ties to the Plovdiv–Leningrad mosaic in the centre.

The rectorate building of the university has a large sgraffito (scratched plaster) decoration of the 1970s–80s. It is in use. The sgraffito is the reason to stop, and it is one of the clearest examples of the “synthesis of the arts” the regime wanted in public buildings.

A steel-framed sports hall (about 2,200 tonnes of steel) on Karlovsko shose, beside Ribnitsa park. Early reports called it a possible ruin; it is not, and national volleyball finals were held there in April 2026. In 2023 the city agreed to buy it back for about 5.2 million leva but pulled the council vote.
Keep it as a pass-by and as the gateway to the monument dump, which is behind the same owner's yard on Vasil Levski Street.
zala-stroitel.s: marica.bg; BTA photos (Apr 2026); D1 research pass

p: Behind a wire fence in the yard of the former Metalni Konstruktsii company, on Vasil Levski Street in Sheker mahala, lie the statues that Plovdiv removed from its streets in 1991–96. A bronze Georgi Dimitrov lies in the grass with other partisan statues, some in pieces, and horses graze on the field. Some were dropped from cranes; one statue is missing an arm and Dimitrov's head is half cut.

They were collected by the sculptor Georges Trak, whose company Tracart and the Union of Artists have a studio there. It is the opposite of Budapest's Memento Park: no signs, no tickets, no guide, just the objects and a fence. You can only look through the wire.

The exact gate has not been found and nobody has confirmed whether you can go in, so treat this as an on-arrival check. The Plovdiv Commune monument (Viktor Todorov, 1970) was said to have ended up in another monument firm's yard on the Rogoshko shose, but no 2020s source confirms it.
monument-dump.s: marica.bg (22 Apr 2023); bntnews.bg (2014); manual pass (28 Oct 2026). Pin approximate; state unverified.

p: A 1970 bus station by the Filipovo railway station that looks closed and is not quite: a visitor in July 2026 reported that the building seems shut but buses still run, with tickets sold by drivers. It is a good example of 1970s transport architecture, and it is at risk: the city council held an extraordinary session on the north and south stations on 4 May 2026.
Behind it is the Filipovo industrial zone, with a 1915 station and half-collapsed old buildings (see next stop). Go soon if you want to see it as it is.
sever-station.s: Google reviews (July 2026); BTA; podtepeto.com; D1 research pass

filipovo-zone.t: Filipovo station and old industrial zone
p: Half-collapsed buildings around the 1915 Filipovo station, which is itself ordinary. The old industrial zone behind the bus station is the nearest thing in the city to a ruin you can see from the street. Keep to the street; the buildings are unsafe.

A football ground in Kyuchuk Parizh, built in 1925–26 and rebuilt in 1984–86, reported in recent reviews as neglected and falling apart, awaiting renovation. Earlier sources conflict between decay and construction. A decaying stadium is a good place to feel how big the socialist sports programme was.

A memorial complex for the September 1923 uprising, on Peshtersko shose 149 in the Smirnenski district, with a mosaic by Georgi Boyadzhiev and the architect Antoaneta Topalova from about 1983. It is not at Kemera, as some sources assumed. It is unmaintained: graffiti, moss and flaking tesserae. A good place to see what the regime's commemorations look like after they lost their audience.

A natural-stone mosaic from the 1980s on Knyaz Aleksandar I Street, number 44, given to Plovdiv by artists from its twin city of Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). It is stable but partly hidden by shop awnings, so look up.
It is the sort of thing that you could walk past a hundred times: a gift of friendship between two cities, from a time when twinning was part of foreign policy.

A Cold War tunnel at the south foot of Bunardzhik Hill, one of two shelters in Plovdiv kept in order. It was reopened in 2026 as a venue for an exhibition on “Lost Spaces” and a public talk on 12 September 2026. It is not open day to day.

Plovdiv has a network of shelters cut into its hills, built for civil defence in the 1950s–60s. This one is the best known, and the one you are most likely to get into if you watch for events. The exact door is not published.
bunardzhik-shelter.s: podtepeto.com (2026); manual pass. Event-only; pin approximate.

p: Three shelters in the hill under the clock tower. The civil-defence education centre behind Radio Plovdiv is open only during the annual civil-defence competition. The shelter next door is a working restaurant. The “Skalata” shelter, formerly under a pastry shop, is abandoned and its entrance a dump.
There is no official register of the shelters; the information comes from a 2025 podtepeto survey. From outside you see doors and rock; the point is to know what is behind them.
sahat-shelters.s: podtepeto.com (4 Mar 2025); D1 research pass. Pin approximate.

p: A rock-face shelter by the Monday market (Ponedelnik pazar) at the foot of Dzhambaz Tepe, once a cave restaurant. It is closed and locked. A second shelter, “Nonstop”, by the cathedral in the Old Town, is also locked. Look at the rock face; do not try the doors.

A large cemetery east of the centre, with different communities side by side: Orthodox, Armenian, Catholic, Jewish and Muslim, plus war graves. For a visitor who is interested in history it is one of the richest places in Plovdiv, and it is open daily from about 07:00 to 21:00.

The Armenian Genocide memorial (1965, by Hazaros Bedrosyan) stands in a 1923 domed-chapel precinct. There is a Catholic war chapel from 1920, Soviet war graves (44 Second World War dead and an obelisk-ossuary from the war of 1877–78), and a British First World War cemetery. In plot 50A are Nayden Gerov, the first mayor, and Captain Raycho Nikolov, the only victim of the 1885 Unification.

The cemetery also has the House of the Deceased, the regime's civil funeral hall, the last of its four secular ritual buildings (see Lotus Hall). A Roma family tomb in a concrete arch, called the “Tsar Kiro” tomb, was reportedly ordered demolished; its state is unconfirmed.
central-cemetery.s: bg.wikipedia (Централен траурен парк); lostinplovdiv.com; D1 research pass; manual pass

p: Stone reliefs at both ends of the road tunnel below the Old Town. At the south entrance a large relief of Hebros and Thrace, from a project by Anastasia Kmetova. On the north side are Philip of Macedon, an ancient temple, Orpheus, the Thracian horseman and a lion with a key as cornerstone. Some are partly overgrown.
tunnel-reliefs.s: lostinplovdiv.com (21 Apr 2026). Pin is the south portal, from a bus stop.

p: A set of sgraffiti (scratched-plaster murals) on Saborna Street and nearby, including the Zahari Zograf and Orpheus panels (early 1970s, Dimitar Kirov, called Di Kiro), a Thracian rider over the Encho Pironkov house, and a 10 by 13 metre wall by Georgi Bozhilov (1968) next to the Church of the Assumption. They are visible from the street. Plovdiv put art on its old streets as well as its new blocks.

Mosaics by Yoan Leviev (1969) in the underpass at Tsar Boris III Obedinitel 54, beside the Chifte Hamam. They were restored in 2020 and have had paint and dirt on them since. It is a small, free, daily-use art gallery that thousands of people walk through without looking.
The same underpass system also shows Roman mosaics behind glass (see the Thrakart and Irini stops), so a walk along this street goes from 1969 back to the fifth century in a few hundred metres.

A bridge of five 30-metre concrete arches, built in 1930–31 by Kamen Velkov and paid for by donations after the Chirpan earthquake. A twin was built alongside in 2008 with a one-metre gap between them. It is named after a pub from 1934. The pub (1936) is now the Gerdzhika Hotel, with a Chinese restaurant; the bridge is the thing to see.

A concrete pyramid and a stone “Thracian plain” pavement about 9 km west of the city on the Pazardzhik road, built in 1970 to mark where Captain Burago’s cavalry is said to have crossed the Maritsa in January 1878. It was renewed in 2009. There is a rival crossing site in town opposite St George's, and both are claims; the memorial is commemoration rather than proof. For completists only.
burago-ford.s: D2 research pass; manual pass. Ford site disputed.

p: A shopping mall stands where Plovdiv's “seventh hill” used to be. Markovo Tepe was quarried away for syenite paving stones, and you have walked on it if you have walked on the city's cobbles. There is nothing to see on the spot except the mall; the interest is the missing hill.
Plovdiv is known as the city of seven hills, and this is the one the city ate. The mall also has a photo chronicle of the hill's history.
markovo-tepe.s: Wikipedia; manual pass. Pass-by: little to see.

roman-stadium-shop.t: Roman stadium in a shop basement
p: A section of the Roman stadium of Philippopolis, the long racetrack under the main street, is said to be visible inside a shop near Dzhumaya Square. Verify on the spot; the research flagged this as unconfirmed. Much more of the stadium lies under the pedestrian street, with the best-known part on display at the north end of the main street.
A communist-era children's railway with four wagons on Youth Hill, seasonal and with unverified running days. The Pioneer railways were a standard piece of the regime's youth programme.

An open-book relief by the sculptor Viktor Todorov on the colonnade of Knyaz Aleksandar I Street, near the spot where the priest Nikola Belchov was hanged in July 1876 after the April Uprising was crushed. The bronze head was stolen and then returned.

Sources give three different dates for the hanging (15, 17 and about 23 July 1876), plausibly calendar or reporting differences, so “July 1876” is the safe form. The plaque sits beside the Roman stadium, which makes the small spot a layered one.

jewish-school.t: Former Jewish school and Monument of Gratitude
p: On 10 March 1943 the Bulgarian authorities began rounding up Plovdiv's Jews for deportation, and held them in the yard of this school. Metropolitan Kiril of Plovdiv climbed into the yard and vowed to lie on the railway tracks if the deportation went ahead. A plaque marks the school and a 1998 monument of a shofar, the Monument of Gratitude, stands in the square.

Bulgaria's Jews inside the pre-war borders were not deported, thanks to a mix of public protest, church and parliamentary intervention, and royal hesitation; the Jews of Thrace and Macedonia, under Bulgarian administration, were deported and killed. Sources differ on how many people were held in Plovdiv, giving about 1,500 people or about 600 families. The stop is quiet and easy to miss.
It is a few steps from the Zion synagogue and the Lotus Hall, so the three can be one short loop.
jewish-school.s: bntnews.bg; bg.wikipedia (Еврейско училище); lostinplovdiv.com. Headcount differs between sources. Pin approximate.

p: A synagogue built in 1886–87 and used as a warehouse under communism. Plaques honour Metropolitan Kiril and Dimitar Peshev, the deputy speaker of parliament who intervened to stop the deportations. It is reached through a courtyard from Eliezer Kalev Street; Google lists Monday–Friday 10:00–13:00, and one visitor reported no free passage. Ask first.
synagogue.s: plovdivtime.bg; Google; manual pass. Address and access differ between sources.

p: A twin-domed Ottoman bathhouse of 1582, with reused Roman stones in its walls and incised builders' drawings, on Boulevard 6 Septemvri. It is one of the best Ottoman buildings in Plovdiv and for a long time worked as a gallery.

It has been closed since 2023 for structural risk, damp and falling plaster, and repairs have been delayed by the heritage procedure. Earlier reports of a working gallery are out of date. For now you can see only the exterior.
The stretch from here to the underpass and back to the Roman mosaics is the best place in the city to see the layers one on top of another.
chifte.s: Capital (Dec 2023); bg.wikipedia (Чифте хамам); D2 research pass; manual pass

p: A fire-gutted shell of a 15th–16th-century Ottoman bath at the corner of Ruski and 6 Septemvri, west of the Dondukov garden. A demolition order of 1929 was never carried out. It sat for years with an illegal billboard on it and was the subject of a court fight.

The hamam gave its name to the Orta Mezar neighbourhood, once the Jewish quarter, which was walled and had three synagogues; the Kalev houses sheltered the revolutionary Levski. (An earlier report called it a furniture warehouse; that was a mix-up with another bath.)
orta-mezar.s: kapana.bg; plovdivtime.bg; podtepeto.com; manual pass. Pin approximate.

p: On Boulevard Bulgaria, to the right of the Hotel Sankt Peterburg, stood a raw-concrete labyrinth by Viktor Todorov from the 1980s on the site of the old gallows, for the political prisoners killed there. The prison building next to it (1878–1963) is reportedly now an office of the water utility ViK-Sever.

The sculptor's own site says the bronze figure is gone, most of the walls are demolished, and a private building was going up. A 2026 memoir describes children climbing on what is left. Treat it as a remnant that may be gone, and look before you go out of your way.
prisoners-memorial.s: viktortodorov.eu; socbg.com (Aug 2026); bg.wikipedia (Затвор – Пловдив). May be gone. Pin approximate.

p: A statue of the jazz violinist Sasho Sladura by the Music Academy and the Ancient Theatre. He was a dissident musician who died in the Lovech labour camp in 1961. You can sit on his knee, and people do.

A rumour that he survived and was a KGB agent circulates; treat it as legend. The statue is in the Old Town's modern memory: a free, human-scale monument to a victim of the regime, a hundred metres from the Roman theatre.
sladura.s: D2 research pass; lostinplovdiv.com. KGB-survival story is a legend.

p: A wooden clock tower on this spot by 1611, rebuilt in stone in 1809–12, with a Viennese clock from 1883. It is 17–17.5 metres high, among the oldest of its kind in Europe, and was the model for the towers at Tryavna, Karlovo and Karnobat. It is open from about 08:00 to 18:00.
The hill under it is full of the shelters on this map; the clock is the Ottoman and Revival-era layer that sits on top.

The only pharmacy museum in Bulgaria, opened in 1981 at Saborna 16, in an Old Town house. Sources give its opening date as 1872 or 1882. Open Tuesday–Sunday. The first Plovdiv pharmacy was said to be from 1845, but no spot has been found.

A stretch of Roman aqueduct in the middle of the Komatevsko shose road. Height and date are disputed between sources (up to about 14 metres per one source, 6–8 per another; 5th–6th century against 2nd–3rd). It is free and by the road, so take care with traffic.
aqueduct.s: ramplovdiv.com; D2 research pass. Height and date disputed.

eastern-gate.t: Eastern Gate and Hadzhi Hasan mahala
p: The Eastern Gate of the Roman and later city wall at Aleksandar Malinov Square, with the 15th-century Hadzhi Hasan mahala (neighbourhood) next to it, still with horse carts. It is free, open about 07:00–18:30, and the quietest of the old-town gates.
The Hadzhi Hasan area is an old Ottoman enclave that now sits right against the modern city. It marks where this map's walks meet the old city.

A late-antique building with mosaics shown in place inside a road underpass at Tsar Boris III Obedinitel 89. It is open daily 09:00–18:00 and costs about €2–3.50. The concrete underpass and the Roman floor share one space, which is the whole of Plovdiv in one room.
irini.s: Manual pass (28 Oct 2026); Google. Prices change.

p: Roman mosaics behind glass walls in the Tsar Boris III underpass, in the Thrakart (Tracart) cultural centre, which belongs to Georges Trak, the sculptor who collected the dumped statues. You can see them from the underpass.
thrakart.s: Lonely Planet; manual pass. Pin approximate.

p: A pile of stones in the Dondukov garden, put there in 1997 as a protest by an artist or group against the state of the garden. It is on the Hristo G. Danov Street side. It is probably still there, but is expected to be removed when the garden is renovated, which had not begun by April 2026. A restoration was promised in January 2025.
Go while it lasts. A protest monument from the 1990s, in a city of regime monuments, is a different kind of memory.
gramada.s: podtepeto.com; lostinplovdiv.com (2026). Expected to be removed. Pin approximate.

p: A bust in the Dondukov garden by Viktor Todorov (1969) of Captain Burago, the Russian cavalry officer credited with freeing Plovdiv in January 1878. Free; a minor stop.

A statue by Danko Dankov (2000) of Kamen Vichev, a Catholic priest shot in 1952, in the garden opposite Sveta Petka on Boulevard Maria Luiza. It may be unlabelled. Plaques have been reported but not confirmed.
kamen-vichev.s: plovdiv24.bg (2026); D2 research pass. Pin approximate.

p: A 2005 plaque at the Dzhumaya mosque for Captain Raycho Nikolov, the only victim of the 1885 Unification; his grave is in plot 50A of the Central Cemetery. A minor stop.
raycho-nikolov.s: D1 and D2 research passes. Pin approximate.

p: The building of the Regional History Museum at Saedinenie Square was built as the assembly hall of Eastern Rumelia by Montani, but the assembly never used it. In September 1885 rebels surrounded the governor's residence and arrested Governor Krastevich on 6 September; no surviving building has been identified as that residence. Open Monday–Saturday.
A row of pines on Bunardzhik said to have been planted in the 1960s by cosmonauts including Gagarin and Tereshkova. The research calls it probable, not confirmed. Pair it with Alyosha.

The former Second Police Station, built in 1904 and a police station from 1938, at Lady Strangford and Antim I streets. Now flats, decaying. On the Antim I side a pre-1944 street sign survives; fewer than 20 such signs are estimated to remain in the city.
The place where a Persian (Adzhemsko) coffeehouse once stood, off Rayko Daskalov and Bogoridi streets. Nothing remains; it is the spot only, and a quick stop on the way.

The Grand Café Kristal was the socialist-era writers' haunt of Plovdiv, a place for Gencho Stoev, Konstantin Pavlov and the actors of the Drama Theatre. It is described in a memoir, Georgi Raychevski's Grandkafe Kristal (1998). Today the building is a rock bar, Download.

The bar leaves this address on 31 December 2026 and the building is for sale, so go before then if you want to sit where they sat. Google pins it at Lady Strangford 5, about 150 metres from the first estimate.
kristal.s: plovdivtime.bg; plovdiv24.bg; podtepeto.com; G. Raychevski, Grandkafe Kristal (1998)

p: A café on Vazrazhdane Square from the 1880s where the poet Petko Rachev Slaveykov drank his morning coffee; the original hearth survives. It closed in March 2026 for restoration, with no reopening date.
starinnoto.s: Master research pass; podtepeto.com. Pin approximate.

p: A gazebo of 1913 where the writer Ivan Vazov spent his last birthday in 1920, in the yard of the Lichev house on Veliko Tarnovo Street. It is a private yard and access is unverified.
vazov-gazebo.s: Master research pass. Access unverified; pin approximate.

p: An 18th-century house with painted alafranga niches, a restaurant that was a bohemian haunt in the 1960s, at K. Nektariev 17. The first research pass wrongly listed it as gone; it is open. It is the best place on this map to sit down in a thinkers' tavern that still works.
Built in 1929 by the architect Boyan Chinkov at Otets Paisiy 28, this was a haunt of bohemians and the intelligentsia. It is open today as a Thai kitchen.

shumen-beerhouse.t: Site of the First Shumen Beerhouse (now Unico)
p: The First Shumen Beerhouse opened in 1913 at Otets Paisiy and General Gurko streets, and the intelligentsia met here after theatre premieres. It is now the restaurant Unico.
A bronze of the painter Tsanko Lavrenov on a bench at Saborna 41, holding a picture frame. Free; sit beside him.

The great saucer-shaped Communist Party hall on Buzludzha peak (1,441 m), built 1974–81 to a design by Georgi Stoilov and one of the most photographed ruins in the world. In 2026 the exterior is free, the interior is sealed, and the site is guarded, with cameras, and asbestos inside. A Getty-funded conservation project by the Buzludzha Project Foundation is under way, and an Open Buzludzha festival was held on 14–16 August 2026.
It is a long day trip: about two hours by bus via Kazanlak, then a taxi or car. Private tours cost from about €270 per vehicle. Go in good weather; the summit is often in cloud.

The best find of the manual pass: a 60-metre stone-and-brick complex on Vlasevitsa hill, 1976, by the Bratska Mogila team (Shinkov, Rangelov and the sculptor Dalchev), with stepped terraces and reliefs, a bell tower, a light well and a crypt with an empty sarcophagus. The crypt is locked but the hill is open day and night. It is about 20 km south-west of Plovdiv and needs a car or taxi.

A branch of the National Military History Museum at the old airfield of Krumovo, with about 66 aircraft outdoors, radar, a 1912 Bozhinov plane and a capsule of cosmonaut Georgi Ivanov. Open Wednesday–Sunday 09:00–18:00. About 12 km south-east; the old Plovdiv airport terminal is nearby, disused since 2009.

A state pulp combine founded in 1952, idle since a fire on 24 September 2024 and closed in 2025, sold to a Plovdiv firm. View it from the road. It is the best large industrial ruin in the region, but an industrial site with new owners, so keep out.
A 1977 concrete flag monolith on three pillars with giant figures and an ossuary, on a hill at Stara Zagora, about 100 km east. Free; hours unverified.
A 1976 hillside memorial complex above Panagyurishte for the April Uprising of 1876, with a giant figure called Borimechkata. Free; about 70 km north-west.
Bulgaria's first socialist town, begun in 1947, with a Stalinist centre, a town hall of 1967 and a museum of “socialist construction”. Hours of the museum are unverified. About 100 km east.

routes.name: West: Bratska Mogila and the rowing canal
routes.when: Bratska Mogila's locked hall may have a caretaker nearby; the rowing canal is a park.
routes.summary: The mound, the Roman aqueduct in the middle of a road, the September Uprising mosaic, the rowing canal, and Burago's ford memorial if you have a car. Long distances: a bike or taxi between stops.

routes.name: Hills: Youth Hill, Markovo Tepe and Bunardzhik
routes.when: The Bunardzhika shelter opens only for events.
routes.summary: The brigade-built cube road, the children's railway, the quarried hill under the mall, the shelter, the cosmonaut pines and Alyosha. A climb, with the best views of the city.

routes.name: Concrete centre: Tobacco Town to the library
routes.when: The library reading rooms are weekdays; Kino Kosmos is a building site.
routes.summary: Tobacco Town, the Youth House, the House of Science, Kino Kosmos, Central Square and the library, with the Design Organisation building, the 1885 museum and the Unification monument as add-ons, and Spartak stadium if you want a long walk south.

routes.name: Main street and Sahat Tepe: the quiet memory layer
routes.when: The clock tower closes in the evening; Rock Bar Download leaves its address on 31 December 2026.
routes.summary: The Roman stadium, Kristal, the Dzhumaya plaque, Belchov, the House with the Tower, the clock tower, the shelters under it and the Leningrad mosaic.

routes.name: Old Town east: tunnels, sgraffiti and taverns
routes.when: The Hippocrates museum is closed on Mondays.
routes.summary: The underpass layers (Irini, Thrakart), the tunnel reliefs, Zlatna Krusha and the beerhouse site, Vazov's gazebo, the Mother and Child House, Kamen Vichev, Sladura, the pharmacy museum, the sgraffiti, Lavrenov, Alafrangite and the Eastern Gate.

routes.name: Dondukov garden: the ritual houses and the Jewish quarter
routes.when: The synagogue is Monday–Friday 10:00–13:00 and reached by a courtyard; the garden's protest heap may be removed.
routes.summary: Lotus Hall, the House of the Newlyweds, the protest heap, Burago's bust, the Orta Mezar ruin, the Jewish school and the synagogue.

routes.name: North of the centre: Chifte, Starinnoto and the Central Cemetery
routes.when: Chifte and Starinnoto are closed (exteriors only); the cemetery is open about 07:00–21:00.
routes.summary: The café site, the coffeehouse spot, the Chifte Hamam, the Leviev underpass mosaics, then a longer walk east to the Central Cemetery.

routes.name: Karshiyaka: the north bus station to the monument dump
routes.when: The monument dump can only be viewed through a fence; the bus station is half-closed but running.
routes.summary: Sever station, the Filipovo ruins, the Big Giant block, Zala Stroitel, the dumped statues, the political prisoners' memorial, Hotel Sankt Peterburg, the food-technology sgraffito and the Gerdzhika bridge.

routes.name: The Fair: Gagarin, Mercury and the river hotel
routes.when: The fair grounds are open during events.
routes.summary: The Gagarin wall, the fair pavilions and the Mercury mosaic, and the Hotel Maritsa.

routes.name: Trakiya: the estate
routes.when: A bus or taxi from the centre.
routes.summary: The estate centre, the block 15 mosaics, the polyclinic fountain, and the disused railway strip (location unverified).

tours.name: The four rites: socialist ritual houses
tours.intro: The regime built secular replacements for church rites: a house for naming the newborn, one for weddings, one for mothers, one for funerals.
tours.how: Lotus Hall and the Newlyweds are side by side in the Dondukov garden; the Mother and Child House is a short walk east; the funeral hall is at the Central Cemetery, a taxi or a long walk.
story: The manual pass found the pattern: the regime did not only close churches, it built ceremonial buildings to take over baptism, marriage, motherhood and burial. Two of the four have since been turned into kitsch exhibits.

stops.note: The 1973 House of the Newborn, now a dinosaur “cave”.
The 1962 glass wedding house; the lower floor is an “Africa” exhibit.
The Mother and Child House; present use unknown.
Holds the House of the Deceased, the civil funeral hall.

tours.name: Mosaics and sgraffiti: art for the people
tours.intro: The regime put art on housing blocks, underpasses and old streets. Plovdiv has more of it than most cities, much of it unlooked-at.
tours.how: Four clusters: Trakiya by bus, the Fair and underpasses on foot, Saborna in the Old Town, and the memorials on a longer ride.
story: A register of Plovdiv's postwar mosaics (novotonasledstvo.eu) gave exact locations and conditions. Leviev, Kmetova, Di Kiro and Bozhilov appear again and again.

stops.note: Anastasia Kmetova, 1973; restored.
A 3-D mosaic fountain, 1980s.
Yoan Leviev, 1971: a spaceman, three dates and a hole.
Leviev, 1969; restored 2020.
A gift from Leningrad artists in the 1980s.
Di Kiro and Bozhilov, 1968–early 1970s.
A large sgraffito on the rectorate.
The September Uprising mosaic, about 1983; unmaintained.

tours.name: Who the state killed, and how Plovdiv remembers them
tours.intro: Plovdiv marks 1876, 1943, the Stalin years and the communist era's victims: some with plaques, some with statues, some with nothing.
tours.how: Mostly the old centre on foot; the prisoners' memorial and the monument dump are across the river in Karshiyaka.
story: The richest theme in the D2 pass: places marked for 1876, 1878, 1925, 1943 and the communist era. Some memorials are neglected, some are gone.

stops.note: The priest hanged in July 1876; the plaque's bronze head was stolen and returned.
10 March 1943: the yard where Metropolitan Kiril stopped the deportation.
Plaques to Kiril and Peshev.
A jazz violinist who died in the Lovech camp in 1961.
A Catholic priest shot in 1952.
The 1953 revolt: no plaque.
The gallows site; may be gone.
The statues the city removed after 1989.
A 1997 protest heap in a garden.

tours.name: Under the hill and under the road
tours.intro: Plovdiv is built on top of itself. Roman floors in an underpass, a stadium under the main street, and Cold War shelters cut into the hills.
tours.how: Mostly in the centre; check event dates for the Bunardzhik shelter.
story: The Roman layer is for looking at; the Cold War layer is mostly locked. Few of the shelters are open, so the map shows where they are and why.

stops.note: Late-antique mosaics inside a road underpass.
More Roman mosaics behind glass.
The Roman stadium; a section is said to show in a shop.
A Roman aqueduct in the middle of the road.
Three shelters under the clock tower.
A locked cave shelter by the market.
Opened for events in 2026.

tours.name: Where the writers drank
tours.intro: From Slaveykov's morning coffee to the Kristal of the 1960s: the cafés, taverns and statues where Plovdiv's writers and actors sat.
tours.how: All in the centre and Old Town. Alafrangite is the one to sit down in; Kristal leaves its address on 31 December 2026.
story: Category C was thin after the first pass; a manual pass of 29 October found Alafrangite open and added Zlatna Krusha, the Shumen beerhouse site and the Lavrenov statue.

stops.note: Slaveykov's café; closed for restoration.
The 1960s writers' haunt; leaves its address 31 Dec 2026.
An 18th-century house and 1960s bohemian haunt; open.
1929, a haunt of bohemians; now a Thai kitchen.
1913; the intelligentsia after premieres.
The painter on a bench.
Vazov's last birthday, 1920; private yard.

tours.name: Ottoman baths, a clock tower and the Unification
tours.intro: Two hamams, one saved and shut, one burnt; a clock tower from the 17th century; and the 1885 Unification.
tours.how: On foot in the Old Town and the centre.
story: The Chifte and Orta Mezar baths are the best small objects of the Ottoman layer. The clock tower and the Eastern Gate carry the story to the Revival, and the museum building shows 1885.

stops.note: 1582; closed since 2023.
A burnt shell of a 15th–16th-century bath.
Wooden by 1611; stone 1809–12; clock 1883.
The gate and the Hadzhi Hasan mahala.
The 1885 Assembly building, never used by the assembly.
The cavalry officer of 1878.

tours.name: From Stalinist blocks to late brutalism
tours.intro: A walk through the regime's styles: Stalinist hotel, 1960s modernism, the Party House, 1970s concrete and the last statements of the 1980s.
tours.how: Mostly the centre on foot; Karshiyaka and Trakiya need a bus or taxi.
story: The Hotel Trimontium (1956) and the Party House (1969) bracket the era. Kino Kosmos, the Youth House and the House of Science are its concrete middle, and Trakiya and the Big Giant show how most people lived.
